new_statements.quote: The basic pattern for stress in the word is to build a binary trochaic foot with a heavy nucleus. This forms a foot with two moras in monosyllables [μμ] and three moras in disyllables—a heavy trochee [[μμ]μ]. The basic rule can be stated most simply that all foot heads must have branching nuclei. [p.68] ... Proclitics in Zapotec bear no stress of their own and are realized consistently with light CV structure. Like proclitics, enclitics cannot be pronounced alone. They are unstressed [p.69] ... Unlike Zapotec stress, which is not lexically contrastive but is instead rhythmical in function, Spanish stress is phonemic (lexically contrastive). [p.72]

new_statements.relation_note: new: nothing on record (no catalog record, no statement held by the project for asun1236). First first-hand statement: Sicoli 2007 sec. 3.3 describes word stress jointly for his two field Zapotec languages, Lachixio AND Asuncion (Mixtepec) Zapotec: one primary stress per phonological word, on the root, realised as a non-iterative heavy trochee (root-initial syllable of disyllabic roots heads the foot; stressed vowel lengthened or following fortis C geminated), clitics never stressed, stress not lexically contrastive ('rhythmical'), no secondary stress; lexical contrast is carried by pitch accents (H, L, LH, HL, unmarked mid) anchored to the stressed root. This corrects the earlier second-ha…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In Lachixio and Asuncion (Mixtepec) Zapotec each phonological word has exactly one primary stress, on the lexical root: the root forms a single non-iterative trochaic foot whose head must be heavy (monosyllabic root CVV = two moras; disyllabic root = heavy trochee with the FIRST root syllable as head, made heavy by vowel lengthening before a lenis C or by geminating a following fortis/sonorant C). Proclitics and enclitics are unstressed and wrap around the stressed root ([[proclitic [STRESSED ROOT]] enclitic]). Stress is predictable/rhythmic, not lexically contrastive; lexical contrast is instead carried by pitch accents (high, low, rising LH, falling HL, or unmarked mid) associated left-to-right from the start of the stressed morpheme, so the language is a lexical pitch accent (tonal) language with root stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None in Zapotec: 'Spanish stress differs significantly from Zapotec stress in that Spanish has secondary stress.' (p.73) and 'Zapotec pronunciations of Spanish loanwords that do not have secondary stress' (p.74); the foot is explicitly 'Non-iterative' (Figure 3.3 caption, p.68).
new_statements.exceptions: Clitics (proclitic classifiers/inflection, enclitic pronouns) never bear stress and stay light CV; only one 'double segment' (geminate/long V) per phonological word, marking the stressed root; glottal stop does not count as a coda consonant for the weight rule (p.66-67); words with an underlying coda nasal/resonant (Lachixio inza 'water', endo 'child', arki 'heart') show no gemination because the X slot is already filled (p.67); contour accents (LH, HL) only on stressed monosyllables (p.95). No lexical exceptions to stress placement are given: stress is stated to be non-contrastive.
new_statements.identity_note: Asunción Mixtepec Zapotec [zoo], asun1236 (INALI 'zapoteco de Valles, oeste'; town of Asunción Mixtepec, mun. San Bernardo Mixtepec, Zimatlán district), a moribund variety inside Sicoli's PhD field region (Sicoli 2021: 3-4); the dissertation's descriptive prosody chapters are reported second-hand to concern Lachixío Zapotec [zpl].

tone_statements.citation: Sicoli, Mark A. 2007. Tono: A linguistic ethnography of tone and voice in a Zapotec region. PhD dissertation, University of Michigan. 231 pp. (ProQuest AAT 3253401; hdl 2027.42/126557)
tone_statements.quote: Zapotec pitch accents are based in a two-tone contrast that specifies high tone and low tone. There is also the unmarked case of the mid level to produce a five-way contrast in monosyllabic words. [...] Lachixío and Asunción Zapotec pitch accent systems are very similar. Each contains an inventory that includes a high accent, low accent, and a combination of low and high that produces a rising accent, a combination of high and low that produces a falling accent, and the absence of accent marking that defines a mid-level pitch.

sources.note: Uses Asunción Mixtepec Zapotec as comparative evidence for early Zapotecan tone -- reports (after Sicoli 2007: 92-94) an underlying per-TBU inventory /H, L, Ø/ for Asunción Mixtepec (tonelessness only in unstressed syllables and grammatical words), notes that Asunción Mixtepec, like Isthmus, Sierra Juárez and Lachixío, allows two-tone melodies split over the syllables of a disyllable (HL on 'meat', LH on 'snake'), and uses the Asunción HL melody to reconstruct Proto Trochaic Zapotec *kwéʔlàʔ 'meat'.
